title: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard -- Ch. 3: Attributes of a Good Judge
keywords: Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard
Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.
"Faith Brought Me to the Supreme Court"
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- an inspirational message to trial judges arguing that the foremost attributes of a good judge are four "Ins": integrity, independence, industry and intelligence.

The permanent exposure of front-line judges to temptation, blackmail, political pressure and kinship appeals, and the conclusion that in the end judges must rely on their own personal attributes and commitments to repel them.

A three-part daily discipline CJP recommends for preserving those attributes: carrying and rereading the Canons of Judicial Ethics and Code of Professional Responsibility, keeping a Bible (or Koran or other book of faith) at hand, and saying a short prayer every day.

The ascetic, self-limiting life the judicial office demands -- divesting oneself of professional, business, civic and social entanglements -- and the spiritual grounding CJP himself draws on, closing with the personal prayer he composed on his first day in the Supreme Court.
sub_topics: An apocryphal opening story of the lawyer who offered to sell a judge a brand-new Mercedes Benz for one thousand pesos, and the judge who answered that he was buying two.

The many forms of pressure on the bench -- brazen and subtle, blackmail, political pressure, friendship, kinship and even religious relationships -- and lawyers retained for their judicial connections rather than their advocacy.
The observation that the ultimate question litigants ask counsel is not whether the case is meritorious but whether counsel knows the judge.
Integrity defined as more than honesty toward others: intellectual decency and a deep sense of personal honor, judged by intentions known only to oneself and to God.
Independence illustrated by Earl Warren, derided on appointment as a mere politician, who became the US government's conscience and critic and ended as one of the greatest American chiefs.
Industry as a personal passion for work extending into evenings and early mornings, when judges have the solitude to wrestle with conscience and gather courage.
Intelligence as more than mental agility -- the ability to organize and communicate thoughts in grammatical language and to know basic law and current jurisprudence, law being a jealous mistress.
The renunciations of judicial life: forfeiting past activities, friends and even relatives, divesting professional and business involvements, and restricting social and sports activities.
FIRST recommendation: carry the Canons and the Code, read one provision a day, interpret them strictly and resolve all doubts against oneself, for the sake of self-esteem more than public perception.

SECOND recommendation: keep a Bible (or the Koran or other basic book of faith) in office, home and car, with the example of CJ Davide cutting the Bible at random each morning and CJP's own use of the daily Mass readings.
THIRD recommendation: a short daily prayer, memorized or spontaneous, consisting not only of petition but also of praise and thanksgiving.
The one-sentence summary that the four "Ins" are preserved by observing the Canons, reading the Bible and praying daily, followed by the prayer CJP composed on October 10, 1995.

stances.claim: The foremost attributes of a good judge are four "Ins" -- integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- and these personal qualities, not rules or institutions, are what finally ward off the temptations pressed on the bench.
stances.rhetorical_move: mnemonic enumeration: a memorable four-part formula defined term by term and then pressed as the judge's only reliable defense

stances.claim: These attributes can be preserved and promoted by three daily practices -- strict rereading of the Canons, reading the Bible or one's own book of faith, and a short daily prayer.
stances.rhetorical_move: numbered prescription (FIRST, SECOND, THIRD) closing with a one-sentence summary of the whole message

stances.claim: Judges should interpret the canons strictly and resolve all doubts against themselves, because the diligent observance of the canons matters more for self-esteem and self-dignity than for public perception.
stances.rhetorical_move: inward reframing: ethical strictness justified by the judge's own self-worth rather than by outside scrutiny

stances.claim: Earl Warren shows that a judge becomes an icon not by legal scholarship but by personifying an independent judiciary.
stances.rhetorical_move: biographical proof: a scorned appointee's later greatness offered as evidence for the value of independence

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' reproduced a short inspirational message Justice Panganiban delivered to trial judges. He opened with an apocryphal story: a lawyer with a multi-billion-peso case pending visited a newly inducted judge and, accused of bribery for parking a brand-new Mercedes Benz in the driveway, explained that he was not giving but selling the car for one thousand pesos -- at which the pacified jurist said he was buying two. The joke, he said, demonstrated the temptations pressed on the bench, some brazen and some subtle: blackmail, political pressure, friendship, kinship and even religious relationships, with lawyers often retained for their judicial connections rather than their skill, so that the ultimate question litigants ask is not whether the case is meritorious but whether counsel knows the judge. Because judges must finally rely on themselves, he set out what he called the four "Ins" of a good judge. Integrity meant not merely honesty toward others but intellectual decency and personal honor, judged by intentions known only to oneself and to God. Independence meant freedom from intellectual, mental and emotional bias, illustrated by Earl Warren, mocked on appointment as a mere politician but remembered as the personification of an independent judiciary. Industry meant a passion for work extending into evenings and early mornings, when a judge has the solitude to wrestle with conscience. Intelligence meant organized thought, grammatical expression and current knowledge of law, since law is a jealous mistress. He described the renunciations the black robes require -- of business, associations and social life -- and then recommended three daily practices: rereading the Canons of Judicial Ethics and Code of Professional Responsibility one provision at a time, interpreting them strictly and resolving all doubts against oneself; keeping a Bible or other book of faith at hand, as Chief Justice Davide did in cutting the Bible at random each morning; and saying a short daily prayer of praise as well as petition. He closed by reciting the prayer he had composed on October 10, 1995, his first day in the Court.
